title: Do GLP-1s Increase the Risk of Suicide?
subtitle: No, they don't. But feel free to read this anyway.
body_html:
Welcome to The Frontier Psychiatrists Substack. It’s a newsletter, and a movement, according to me. I’m trying to build support for that idea with the silly newsletter, and I’m thrilled—thrilled—to have you, dear reader, as part of our mission. We endeavor to answer a question that gets me up early, most mornings:

Can we get better outcomes for patients —safer, sooner, and sustainably?

One of the potential agents I’ve highlighted is the class of drugs called GLP-1 drugs—semeglutide, liguratide, tirzepetide, and more coming soon. GLP-1 is short for glucagon-like peptide 1, and these drugs bind to the GLP-1 receptors in the body in a similar way to the natural (“endogenous”) compound. One of these drugs, tirzepetide, also binds as Glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP)—so it does two things at once, like the combo pills for hypertension or “broad-spectrum” antibiotics.

The acquired podcast has a great long-form episode on the history of the first wildly successful of these drugs, Ozempic. It’s suggested.

The task I was given by my dear friend Amir Kalali, M.D., who created the remarkable CNS Summit community, was to join a panel reviewing the potential of these medicines for the treatment of neuropsychiatric illnesses. Here is what I was asked to review, and I’ll share what I learned with you, my readers, today.

  • Depression

  • Anxiety disorders

  • Alzheimer’s disease and cognitive impairment

  • Substance use disorders

  • Parkinson’s disease

  • Eating disorders

  • OCD – compulsive gambling?

  • What indications do not seem to benefit from GLP-1 agonists?

  • Many psychiatric treatments are known to promote weight gain. Are GLP-1 agonists appropriate adjunctive treatments?

  • Suicidal ideation has been reported in GLP-1 trials. Is the exacerbation of suicidality a concern in psychiatry?

  • Can you comment on the relationship between alcohol use and criminal behavior… and the potential for GLP-1s in this space?

So, let’s hope I can cover that in the 30 minutes I have to discuss it. To ruin a surprise, I didn’t get to it all. however, in my attempt to prepare, I got ready to rapid-fire my prep for you, my readers, and give insights into how I think about forming an opinion good enough to share with the world here, on the mildly influential.

When I’m asked, “What do you think?” I have the same answer every time—what does the data say? Who cares what I think?!

When I say “go to the data,” there are several ways to interact with the literature, but I prefer to start with Google Scholar. People often assume I’m using AI for this writing, and I’ve tried a few times, but it has gone poorly as a tool for a publication with a very educated audience. People spell-check and grammar-check—if I published a made-up study? Let’s just say that might fly in corporate or government work, but not here. My readers hunger for the truth, and I’ve built trust. LLMs lie like teenagers who were “just about to shower,” and it takes longer to fact-check their output than to search myself.

Let’s offer an example. Do GLP-1s cause suicidal thinking?

In 2033, European Regulators (the European Medical Association) started a probe into the safety of GLP-1s. This sounds scary:

EMA’s safety committee, the PRAC, is reviewing data on the risk of suicidal thoughts and thoughts of self-harm with medicines known as GLP-1 receptor agonists,1 including Ozempic (semaglutide), Saxenda (liraglutide) and Wegovy (semaglutide). These medicines are used for weight loss and for treating type 2 diabetes.

Let’s dig in. I chose, somewhat at random, “suicidality” as the first search term to use:

Let’s look at what happens when I search for GLP-1 “suicide”:

Wow, a few different letters and it’s a totally distinct search! My advice? Do more than one version of the search, and iteratively, you’ll answer questions in a more satisfactory way.

One thing you are noticing, that is empirical, even at this level, is the date of publication. More recent is likely, especially in novel science like this, where many researchers are digging in to be more helpful to your opinion formation! Limiting the search to 2021, as an example:

More recent articles are likely to have larger data sets than older articles, which give me more confidence the results are less likely to be statical flukes.

In the most recent meta-analysis from 2025, the answer to the “do GLP-1s cause suicide” is a resounding no…

[in] 32 354 individuals receiving GLP-1 RAs and 27 042 treated with placebo, over 69 653 and 63 853  person-years of exposure, respectively. Event incidence was very low in the GLP-1 RA (0.047 per 100 person-years) and placebo (0.042 per 100 person-years) groups, with no statistically significant difference (rate ratio [RR], 0.76; 95% CI, 0.48-1.21; P = .25).1

Another very large study from 2024 compared those with treated with GLP-1s and those treated with other medicines for diabetes as a control, and again found no link:

124 517 adults initiated a GLP-1 receptor agonist and 174 036 initiated an SGLT2 inhibitor… During a mean (SD) follow-up of 2.5 (1.7) years, 77 suicide deaths occurred among users of GLP-1 receptor agonists and 71 suicide deaths occurred among users of SGLT2 inhibitors…The HR was 0.83 (95% CI, 0.70-0.97) for suicide death and nonfatal self-harm2

Thanks JAMA Psychiatry and JAMA Internal Medicine. But wait a minute, way back in 2024, another large study, in a different sample, found the opposite!

The analysis spanned data from January 1, 2015, to December 31, 2023. To minimize selection bias, we employed 1:1 propensity score matching to account for demographic factors such as age, sex, race, and comorbidities. After matching, the study included 162,253 case and control patients. This study showed a significant association between GLP-1 RA treatment and an 98% increased risk of any psychiatric disorders. Notably, patients on GLP-1 RAs exhibited a 195% higher risk of major depression, a 108% increased risk for anxiety, and a 106% elevated risk for suicidal behavior.3

To be clear—there are 20+ papers evaluating this question in 2025 alone, and all of them find no increased risk definitively. What I suspect this questions comes down to is sampling error. I’ll demonstrate:

In this sample from Denmark, just by eyeballing it, it looks like GLP-1s don’t increase risk (yellow is GLP-1s, blue is SGLT2 diabetes medicines):

And then you could look at this sample, from the same paper, but collected in Sweden:

And just with the naked eye, it looks like there is MORE risk. The yellow line is higher!

Different samples can—by chance—look very different. Or maybe someone is handing out pro-suicide propaganda in Sweden? I don’t actually know that anyone is doing that, but the population’s baseline propensity for a risk is a crucial factor in any statistical an analysis. Especially in uncontrolled studies, where we are forced to rely on our brains and mathematical approaches like propensity matching, it can be easier to come to erroneous conclusions.

Reviewing all the most recent data helped calm my nerves. However, staying vigilant and skeptical at the same time, with our minds open to changing when new data arises, is crucial to having the best possible relationship with risks to our own health.

Also, I got this great photo taken at CNS Summit!

Thanks, photographer George Lucozzi!

I know, I know. Thanks for reading.

Share

1

Ebrahimi P, Batlle JC, Ayati A, et al. Suicide and Self-Harm Events With GLP-1 Receptor Agonists in Adults With Diabetes or Obesity: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. JAMA Psychiatry. 2025;82(9):888–895. doi:10.1001/jamapsychiatry.2025.0091

2

Ueda P, Söderling J, Wintzell V, et al. GLP-1 Receptor Agonist Use and Risk of Suicide Death. JAMA Intern Med. 2024;184(11):1301–1312. doi:10.1001/jamainternmed.2024.4369

3

Kornelius, E., Huang, JY., Lo, SC. et al. The risk of depression, anxiety, and suicidal behavior in patients with obesity on glucagon like peptide-1 receptor agonist therapy. Sci Rep 14, 24433 (2024). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-024-75965-2
